analysis.one_liner: Guarantees college athletes name, image, and likeness rights, post-graduation injury care, and protected scholarships.
analysis.headline: Introduced June 9, 2025, with one cosponsor, and referred to two House committees with no further action taken.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would write national rules for college athletes' name, image, and likeness (NIL) earnings: no school, conference, or athletic association could bar an athlete from signing an endorsement deal, and standard contracts would be required to be in writing with clear terms. It would also require schools to give athletes financial literacy and career training, pay all medical costs for sports injuries for four years after graduation, and guarantee a scholarship cannot be cut for injury, illness, or roster decisions. The trade: it would declare college athletes are not employees of their schools, bar states from regulating athlete compensation, and shield schools and athletic associations from lawsuits over rules that comply with the bill.
analysis.who_benefits: College athletes on athletic scholarships. They would keep the right to sign endorsement deals, get required training in finances, careers, and mental health, keep their scholarships even if injured or cut from the roster, have up to ten years to finish their degree, and have four years of medical costs covered for injuries suffered playing their sport [S2].

how_it_helps.text: No institution, conference, or athletic association could restrict a student athlete from entering an NIL agreement, and an athlete could not be barred from competing for having an agent [S2]

Schools would have to pay all medical costs for four years after an athlete graduates for any injury sustained playing varsity sports, and could not reduce or cancel a scholarship because of injury, illness, or roster management decisions [S2]
Scholarships would remain available for degree completion for ten years after they are first awarded, even if the athlete stops playing [S2]
Every athletic association would have to maintain a public, searchable database of anonymized deal data so athletes can estimate what their NIL rights are worth before signing [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Colleges and universities, which would bear new costs for post-graduation medical care and guaranteed scholarships and would lose the ability to limit athlete compensation through their associations. State governments would lose their power to set their own NIL and athlete-compensation rules, and athletes would give up any claim to employee status, including unionization and wage claims [S2].

drawbacks.text: The bill states a student athlete may not be considered an employee of a school, conference, or athletic association, permanently closing the door to unionization, workers' compensation, and minimum-wage claims that some athletes have pursued through the courts [S2]
No state could enforce any law governing athlete compensation, employment status, or NIL rights in college sports, wiping out stronger protections some states have already enacted [S2]

Schools and athletic associations that comply with the bill could not be sued under any law for enforcing rules that limit or prohibit compensation paid by the schools and associations themselves [S2]

Schools could still restrict a deal that they judge to negatively impact the institution's reputation or conflict with an existing school contract, and athletes must disclose the terms of their NIL agreements to their school, giving institutions visibility into athletes' private earnings [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The athlete benefits are concrete and substantial: guaranteed medical care after graduation, scholarships that survive injury, and protection from losing eligibility over endorsement deals. But the price is heavy and structural. In exchange, athletes would be locked out of employee status nationwide, states would lose their say, and the schools and associations that govern college sports would get a liability shield. It is best understood as a compromise package: real protections for athletes, paid for by forfeiting their strongest legal claim — that the multibillion-dollar college sports system treats them as employees in everything but name.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in June 2025, sent to the Education and Workforce and Energy and Commerce committees, and has sat there with no hearings, no amendments, and no votes since [S4].

narrative.text: Rep. Lisa McClain, a Republican from Michigan, introduced the bill on June 9, 2025, joined by Rep. Janelle Bynum, a Democrat from Oregon [S1]
It was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee and the House Energy and Commerce Committee for consideration [S4]
The only cosponsor on record is Rep. Bynum, and no committee action, hearing, markup, or vote has been recorded since the referral [S3]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For now, the college sports establishment. The NCAA, athletic conferences, and athletic departments keep the existing system — athletes earn NIL money but have no employee rights — because the bill has gone nowhere and nothing has changed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The college sports establishment, for now

sides.party_line_note: A Republican sponsored it and its sole cosponsor is a Democrat; no committee or floor votes exist yet to show a broader partisan split.

industries.industry: College sports governing bodies (the NCAA and athletic conferences)
industries.note: The bill regulates these associations but locks them in: they would become the official NIL agent-registration gatekeepers and would run the public market-value database, and rules that limit compensation paid by the associations themselves would be shielded from lawsuits. The athlete non-employee rule also protects the existing conference-and-NCAA structure from the biggest legal threat to it [S2]

Schools would take on real new costs — four years of post-graduation medical care for sports injuries, guaranteed scholarships, mandatory training — but would gain federal preemption over state NIL laws and a declaration that athletes are not employees, blocking unionization and wage claims [S2]

Written-contract requirements, disclosure rules, and a public market-value database would make paying athletes more predictable and reduce disputes, so brands and collectives could spend with more certainty [S2]

industries.industry: Athlete agents and NIL marketing agencies
industries.note: The bill bars schools and associations from keeping athletes from getting representation and creates a registration system agents could join, formalizing their role in the market [S2]

analysis.trajectory: Bills that go only as far as referral to two committees and sit with one cosponsor rarely move, and most die when the Congress ends. Unless House leadership makes college sports legislation a priority, this bill is likely to stay parked in committee.
